title: Workshop: Building Agentic Apps End to End with Replit Agent

segments.text: BRANDON MIDDLETON: All right.
So my name is Brandon Middleton.
I'm the Head of Education at Replit.
Clearly, not the head of AV standing up here.
But this talk is about human potential's big moment.
This was about 11 years ago.
I stand in the Guinness Book of World Records
for being the first person to rap--
hip-hop rap.
A commencement speech I did the evening and weekend MBA program.
I graduated in 2015.
If you want to hear the rap, come meet me outside.
Maybe I still remember it after 11 or 12 years.
This talk is about how we can shift,
how we do education and AI literacy in classrooms,
in research, in higher ed and academia.
And if you have thoughts and questions and commentary
about this topic, we're in an experimentation phase.
There's lots of trials to try and things to succeed and fail
at.
So I'll be offstage trying to meet as many
of you who are interested in this topic.
All right.
I deeply believe in the power of education.
I've taught outside of my regular job
at Amazon and at Microsoft and at other places.
And at Replit, I actually got the opportunity
to full time focus on what I've been doing for the last seven
or eight years.
So I get to focus on universities and colleges and K
through 12 and nonprofits that are focusing
on trying to bring AI literacy into a practical and tactical
realm.
So I'll talk a lot about the work that we're doing.
I see some people that I've worked with in the audience
already.
So it's going to be a fun time here.
All right, let's blast off and go.
All right.
So I'm going to try to make this talk like also a demonstration
of how you build an end-to-end application using
a platform like Replit that has agentic AI embedded inside
of it.
Hands up if you've ever used agents or agentic AI
to build anything.
OK, almost the whole room, hands go up.
If you build something today, hands up.
All right.
So if you go to this actual URL here--
I'm afraid to do this because I'm afraid that we'll pop out
again.
But there's an app that I created this morning.
All right.
So if you click that URL, it'll take you
to a page that looks like this.
And if you click that wall, this button here,
there is a picture of all of our new joiners here.
I used Replit agent to actually--
let's see-- build this application out.
Man, this is killing me.
So if you would like to leave a message
or if you would like to literally participate
in this scroll wheel/scroll wall,
this is an example of something that's using agentic AI
and agents in order to build.
It accepts your images or your messages.
And then it will put this scroll wall together in the back
that you'll be able to see.
All right.
All right.
So I'm going to go there.
And looks like you can see all of you
guys' images popping up on the screen there.
Great job and great to meet everybody virtually.
Is this the first, like live demo, demonstration
that you guys have seen today?
No?
OK, you've seen a little bit more.
Well, keep doing this if you like.
Put images, put comments and commentary.
But this is one example of agentic AI at work.
All right.
So let's go back to presentation here and keep going.
All right.
So I've taught at the Stanford Design School.
I teach a class every spring quarter
called Redesigning Finance.
And I've had students joke to me about the state of higher
education, and us calling it that as educators because
of the price of the tuition and not necessarily
how fun it is to be in class or the quality of the content
or the differentiation between being in class
or going to YouTube or going somewhere else
to learn the same kind of information.
So there's a lot of truth in jest sometimes.
You get students to rib you and give you a sense of like, man,
the return on investment, as I believe in the American dream
to get me a job and to do everything
that people have told me to do.
That's starting to wane a little bit.
If you've heard some of that sentiment from students
or if you feel a little bit like that yourself,
give me a hand wave.
There's a few people who are like,
man, it's tougher to get a job, or it's tougher
to believe in the status quo these days.
So I feel like the reason that some of these jokes work
is because there's some truth to this.
We need to actually think about how exactly it
is we're going to reimagine education as a whole, what is it
for, how do we do it, and how do we
build the bridge from higher ed, higher institution of academia,
into the workforce.
Workforce development is a little bit
of what I focus on at the K through 12 level, all
the way through college, and then
into early career at Replit.
All right.
So what we did to try to talk to people in a ground-up fashion
is go on what we're calling an AI literacy tour.
So I've been to Chicago this summer, where I'm from,
born and raised.
I got a 708 number in Michael Jordan's shoes.
That's all I got left from Chicago.
I've been in the Bay Area for 21 years now.
We've been to Chicago.
We've been to New York.
We've been to Los Angeles.
We've been to Atlanta.
We're here in the Bay Area talking
to people about what it feels like to be
a student at this time, what it feels like to be a teacher,
receiving mandates from the top, and trying
to translate AI literacy into something
meaningful for yourself and then for your students and community.
And what we're trying to move towards is an answer
to try to reimagine what education actually looks
and feels like, because in certain places,
I think that it is for sure failing.
All right.
All right.
So the education system, as it currently exists,
is actually designed pretty well.
It was designed hundreds of years ago for a world
that today is not really existent.
Information itself used to be scarce.
So you needed to come to a university in order to actually
receive it from a professor who was the "end all and be all."
You come to receive and retrieve that information
from your professor.
The knowledge was locked up in libraries and laboratories
and lecture halls.
And the world remembered the answer
and used the answer that you were receiving.
It was often the evidence of your learning,
if you knew the actual answer, which is not true today.
You can have a lot of book knowledge and no street smarts.
You can have a lot of things that you've observed,
but maybe that is all misinformation or
disinformation.
So today, information is not scarce literally everywhere.
Answers are abundant.
And increasingly, the intelligence
itself is becoming pervasive and abundant as well.
So how do we move into an intelligence age, where
the cost of the models are dropping,
but the intelligence of the models
is actually getting really, really good?
How do we Replit, and how do we as an industry within education
think about how to wield this intelligence moving forward
for technology and non-technical people who are going
to be using these platforms?
So this massive civilization level shift
creates a big uncomfortable question
for the institution of higher ed.
If we were designing college for today, like summer of 2026,
and we could start with a blank canvas and a blank sheet
of paper, how exactly would we go about doing that?
Will we still organize everything
around lectures in libraries?
And will we create semesters that are 16-weeks long still,
or will we make things shorter?
Will we count attendance?
Does that matter in the future of education?
Closed book recall and rote memorization
of things on final exams, is that a thing
that we need to hold on to or something
that we should throw away?
We've confused time served in college institutions
with learning.
We've confused the credentials with a student's capability
to actually perform.
And sometimes we've confused sorting students
throughout four or five years with actually educating them.
So college has become this extraordinarily expensive
sorting system.
And we sort by admissions.
Sometimes we sort by grades and departments.
Sometimes we're sorting by the actual institution
that that person or those people went to.
And then the result of it at the end of four or five years,
we call merit.
And we literally hire or not hire on the basis of that
sometimes.
So I think a lot about that at Replit.
And what we've been doing on this AI literacy tour
or campaign across these five different cities is literally
asking people, from preschool teachers--
lady in the back is a preschool teacher--
all the way up through researchers and professors
at R1/tier 1 universities, what's happening.
How can we incrementally choose small experiments and things
to peel off and try that might be
useful in defining what education is going
to look like in the future?
So in this session-- this is me in the community
in East Palo Alto.
I live in Palo Alto and do a lot of community work in East Palo
Alto.
And we had a session of seven-year-olds in the room all
the way up to elders, 77-year-olds, in the room.
And we were talking about the issues of resource allocation
and different things that plague the city of East Palo Alto.
And I'm using these sticky notes to put things on paper.
I'm using my phone and applications to actually capture
the things that the seven and eight-year-olds are telling me,
as well as the things that the 75 and 76-year-olds are telling
me.
And I'm using Replit as a platform
to basically-- like you're doing with your photos,
upload that to an application and think with AI as a partner
and show the community exactly how easy it is to do,
even though they themselves didn't identify as computer
scientists and engineers.
All right.
So meanwhile, the work world outside of the community aspect
is sending us some pretty staunch messages.
And a couple of stats for you.
At the beginning of this year, 2026,
unemployment amongst young recent college graduates
was about 5.7%.
So just under 6%.
More strikingly, about 41.5% were underemployed,
meaning that I might have graduated
from a really fancy school, but I
might be working in something that's
really underneath my intellectual capability or even
my interest, which is also a problem.
So we have that to deal with.
This doesn't mean that the college
institution in and of itself doesn't have any value.
It means that the connection between education, student
capability, and opportunity is currently under strain,
and we need to solve for that.
The World Economic Forum reports that nearly 40%
of workers' current skills are expected to change
between this year and 2030.
So that if you had 100 people representing every of the 8
billion people on Earth, 59 out of those 100 people
would literally have to shift and re-skill and re-pivot
within the next four years.
So that's how much change we have to think about.
And that's why I hold everything with a really loose grip,
because everything in AI changes so quickly.
All right.
So if the global workforce is going to change
and a diploma can't be the finish line, what do we do?
Maybe that diploma is not even like the reliable map
that we should be using in the future as we rebuild this thing.
So the real advantage, as I've seen it,
has come from the ability to actually learn,
the ability to unlearn, and the ability to pick things back up
and relearn them as I move forward.
I graduated from UIUC as an electrical engineer.
I came out to the Bay to work at Cisco systems
as a networking software engineer.
And I went to Haas Business School and graduated in 2015.
I started to put down a lot of my technical skills
in terms of programming, in terms of product management
that I used to do.
But these days, I left AWS after six years
to join Replit as the Head of Education.
I'm actually picking back up some
of those skills of product management, some
of those skills within the EPD triangle of design
and engineering and product management,
in order to build experiences for people
that are both technical and non-technical as we
move forward.
So relearning, unlearning, and learning to learn is a really
core skill if you're going to be a contributor to this education
of the 21st and 22nd century.
All right.
So AI is not the next ed-tech gadget.
I see AI a little bit differently
than I see the calculator, for example.
A little bit different than a Google search
engine from 2003 and 2004.
I see it as not only a way to automate things
like grading or summarization of papers
that you might receive as a professor or a way
to generate lesson plans.
But AI gives us, I think, a once-in-a-century opportunity
to actually rebuild education around human potential.
So I think each of us have an innate passion, desire,
skill to be able to do and deliver something to the rest
of the 8-plus billion of us on this planet.
And I think we can use vibe coding
and use agentic AI in order to help humans achieve
peak performance in their fullest potential moving
forward.
For the first time in history, I think
imagining agentic assistants and personal tutors
is a real thing that can be achieved and grasped
within the next couple of years.
All right.
So this is a picture of me in the community again.
This is, if you're not familiar, a guy who was signed
to a record label for 10 years.
Five years ago, he got released from that initial deal
where he did three albums, won a Grammy, and all of that.
He came to the Replit office asking
not so much about agentic AI in technical terms.
But he launched out as an entrepreneur and said, hey,
I want to run a record label and do
a lot of things that plagued me when I was part of the larger
music industry.
Things like revenue recognition for the amount of royalties
I should receive when I stream my music across all
of the different platforms like Spotify or YouTube Music.
You get fractions and fractions of pennies for doing that.
And he would actually go about trying
to audit the money that he would receive.
And the runaround that he described
and the errors and all of the things
that were basically swept under the rug
that most other artists weren't doing, he thinks,
is a big opportunity.
So he's building a new record label
and using vibe coding, even though he hasn't really
got that computer science and that technical background
in order to reimagine things in the music industry.
Even though he's not part of an actual university right now,
this also falls underneath the umbrella of education
in my scope at Replit.
Music education, there's business education,
there's technology education.
So if you've got thoughts around things that typically will
sit outside of the university, I'm
happy to talk with you guys one to one about that as well as I
leave the stage.
All right.
So let's talk about this personal tutor
for every learner.
Not only for wealthy individuals.
A lot of folks that are neighbors of mine in Palo Alto
will send their kids to Saturday school.
Or they get out of school at 3 o'clock,
and they're not home until 6 o'clock
because they've got these personalized tutors for STEM
subjects and for other things.
But I think that students whose parents
know how to navigate the system, that's pretty soft.
But for the ones that are not confident to raise that hand
in a crowded lecture hall, it's cool to think about how we can
use agentic AI to build personal tutors that will be available
24/7 hours a day.
2:00 AM, when that student, who's too shy to raise
their hand in lecture hall, needs a question answered.
Students who need an explanation and an alternative way.
Maybe you're visual and not auditory learner.
Or maybe you perform well in oral exams versus taking
written timed exams.
There's lots of examples of students
that need accommodations and have them
in order to learn at their best.
And the ability to personalize education
without any embarrassment, exhaustion,
or judgment on behalf of the student and the teacher,
who sometimes is in a one-to-many type of forum,
is something that we think a lot about at Replit.
Multilingual support.
Lingual support is something that in the Bay Area--
I lived in Chicago, so I heard a little bit of Spanish,
but mostly English when I came out
of Illinois and towards California.
When I arrived here, pretty much everybody
speaking at least two languages.
I felt like a total slacker for the first several years
of my life.
If you speak more than one language, give me hands up.
So I am underachieving all of you, essentially,
by only speaking English.
But I think agentic AI can really help with that, too.
You can speak into Replit as a platform.
English, just as well as you can do
French or Spanish or any other of your native tongues.
And then have that translated in apps
that you build to other people who
speak different languages on the other side of that interaction.
All right.
So I don't see what we're talking about
as replacing teachers.
I think the teachers themselves have really important work
to do.
So that we're talking about expanding the reach of what
one individual is able to do for a classroom of sometimes 15,
sometimes 50, sometimes hundreds people at a time.
So when the teacher becomes less of a broadcaster
and more of a designer and a coach
and a mentor, a critic, and a community builder,
I think the students have a lot of room to thrive
and a lot of room to grow into leadership and ownership
as they move towards what's next for them.
And AI can definitely deliver the information.
But what the teacher needs to do and why that matters
is a very personal kind of that care, that concern,
that thing that is intangible, a lot of the times,
that belief that the teacher has in that
student that will allow them to stay up
that extra couple of hours and complete something or have pride
in the work that they turn in as a result of the seeds that
were planted in them by that teacher.
All right.
So this is my future.
I've got three startups-- one aged 14, one aged 10,
and 1 aged seven.
Basically, at the end of every pay cycle,
I empty out my wallet to do things that make them happy.
And I think a lot about--
When I get out of bed, I'm excited to contribute
to this future because I know that four years from now,
the oldest startup is going to go into college.
And in 2030, who knows what learning,
what education, what credentialing,
what college, what work even will be?
If you ideas about this and you feel
like you know what's going to happen in 2030,
please see me immediately after this presentation.
So this is special to me in that I think the experimentation
window that we have is about a year, year and a half, maybe two
years, to try all of these things
and see what sticks and see what does not stick.
We have a program that we run at Replit called our Faculty
Fellows Program.
I see one person in the audience that's a part of us.
Dr. [? Chen, ?] wave at everybody.
We do a monthly webinar where people
who have said yes to experimentation
use a Replit platform to build out experiences
and to build out things.
And they put them in front of students.
Or they use them in their research
and then report back to a cohort that's now about 75 teachers
large.
And we talked through what worked, what didn't work.
And we try to share that information in community
so that the next person who is yet
to dip their toe in the water feels a little bit more
comfortable and confident doing that on the back of that shared
experience.
So I'm hoping that my kids see enough at home
and are able to learn enough from these communities that
are building to be confident to experiment themselves
as they go into high school and into college.
All right.
So let me show you the Replit interface.
If you've seen Replit itself before, raise your hand.
OK.
Can I get one volunteer to explain
what Replit is to somebody that's never,
never used it before?
One volunteer from the crowd.
Go ahead, in the black shirt.
AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]
BRANDON MIDDLETON: Explain what Replit is for someone
who's never used it.
AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]
BRANDON MIDDLETON: Oh, who has never used it.
OK.
So you are not the person to answer.
Right here, in the blue shirt.
Yes.
AUDIENCE: So from idea to built AI application
without the [INAUDIBLE].
BRANDON MIDDLETON: Love that.
So he said from idea to built AI application
without the requirement of knowing
much about the technology underneath.
So since you already gave you a hat,
I'm going to give you this to give to somebody else.
Thank you, sir.
AUDIENCE: We want the hat.
BRANDON MIDDLETON: Yeah, you guys can mob him after.
But the actual Replit interface, if I come out of here and--
let's see.
OK here.
All right.
So this is the Replit interface.
I'm going to come over.
All right.
So you get a prompt box like this, which is a very natural--
I've done this with ChatGPT.
I've done this with Claude before.
And essentially, if you click Import here
on the actual screen, if you want
to start from something that you've already been building
in another place, you can import, work from other places,
into Replit.
If you want to check the status of other projects
that you've been working on, as you continue to build out
things in Replit, you'll get a full page
of all of the different things that you've done.
I built this slide presentation in Replit, as you guys know.
Talk about integrations with other pieces of technology
that you probably interact with on a day-to-day basis.
All of the different connectors that we
have are personal and enterprise types of connectors.
So I personally use a lot of Dropbox and Discord
and Slack and Google Drive.
If I scroll all the way down, there
are 511 different integrations that you can be prompting.
And you can say, hey, Replit, go grab my Google Drive,
my Dropbox, and my Databricks and my Google Sheets,
for example.
And I want to make an application that does XYZ.
So it's a lot more fun to connect
into all of these applications before you build the thing
that you want to build out.
All right.
Let's go back here.
Back home.
So the artifact and the output types,
you see website here, mobile app, design, games.
We built that photo app in a few minutes here.
So these are all the different kinds
of artifacts and expressions that you
can put into this prompt box and steer the model towards.
So if you know you want to build a slide deck,
just click the Slide Deck button.
If you know you want to build a mobile app,
iOS, Android, click the Mobile App button,
and that'll steer Replit in the direction that's
necessary in order for you to start that back
and forth interaction.
On the bottom left here, there's a Learn
and a Documentation button, where
we've spent a good amount of time
putting video content together to take people from 0 to 100.
And then from 100, a little bit further.
If you are not familiar with vibe coding,
you're not familiar with building with AI,
the Documentation and some of these Learn apps
are really helpful for that.
OK.
And coming back here.
Once you've actually kicked off an actual work session,
you can see that there's a number of modes.
So there's light mode here, which
allows you to ask very basic questions like, hey,
can you change the color, the background color, of my slides,
from black to orange?
Can you change the text of this slide
to, say, this instead of that?
That's what light mode is for.
Economy mode is like the default middle-of-the-road reasoning,
intelligence.
And then when you want to do things
that are really, really ambitious,
you can go to power mode.
And for each of these, you've got the ability
to click into these and select either closed models
or open models, depending on the level of work
that you're trying to do.
So model choice and the ability to actually choose
the right model for the right thing
that you're asking Replit to do is part of the experience here.
All right.
So that's a little bit about the Replit platform itself.
Let's check on our application here and see
if we've got any new faces.
All right.
Dr. [? Chen, ?] you're looking good there.
Love to see you guys doing that.
All right.
Let's keep going with the actual presentation itself.
Let me come full screen mode here.
And present.
All right.
So let's talk about responsible AI use
and how we can do assessment a little bit differently.
So we have to change the kinds of things that we value.
I think testing is pretty dead at this point.
In my class, Redesigning Finance,
I usually am asking students to YouTube record explanations
five to seven minutes at a time of them
grappling with a topic in finance that we're discussing.
So one of the themes from last year's class was,
how do you deal with catastrophes
like the LA wildfires that happened a couple of years ago?
If you were trying to redesign reinsurance and the insurance
industry and improve the claimants' experience
for the next fire that happens in LA or the next flood that
happens in Florida, how do you actually
go about designing something at the claimant level,
at the insurer level, at the re-insurer level,
and have students literally build stuff and then actually
defend what they've built synchronously?
So unless they've learned how to master deep faking,
they're putting the work into actually thinking through it
and putting a prototype and their video next to it
as a submission.
So I think we should stop designing assessments
around stuff that machines can do well and start designing
with the human being in mind.
And each human being, actually, has different capabilities.
So I, in my own grading, have done some adaptive type of work.
It's all group work.
But we look at the students' grade in school.
So freshman through master's students.
We look at the students' background
in engineering versus I'm a brand-new coder
or a brand-new person to technology.
And we grade across things like the fidelity of the design
that they put forward, the collaboration that they've
showed within the group as measured
by how their teammates are voting,
and not necessarily how we the teachers and we the TAs
look at them.
So these are a couple of ideas about how to change assessment
in terms of moving away from exams or pop quizzes
and more towards experiential and building.
All right.
Taking away judgment, curiosity, care, originality,
and collaboration.
If we remove these things and they're already
absent from the system, I don't think we're setting ourselves
up for success.
So let's lean into empathy.
Let's lean into the ability to frame problems,
worthwhile questions to ask.
Get high points, even if you don't have the answers
to them necessarily, in the classes
that I've been teaching over the last year or two.
All right.
All right.
The question should no longer be, did the student use AI?
But better questions that we should be asking ourselves
as educators are, did the student actually think?
Did the student verify the work that they put forward?
Did they cite sources, say where it came from?
Did the student improve the work?
Did the student explain the decisions and the choices
that they made in order to get to the output
that they actually came to?
Can the student defend the conclusion?
And can the student tell us where
the machine and the machinery actually got it wrong?
They're using their own judgment.
They're using their own expertise in a particular area
to make judgments about what the machine said.
So imagine this oral defense after every major individual
or group project.
Imagine students submitting not only one final answer,
but a tract record of their reasoning.
I built a system inside of Replit
that allows students to actually reflect on
lectures, submit the actual assignments,
and then for them to be able to track again.
The space between two lectures, you might have learned a lot.
The space between one exam and the next exam,
you might have learned a lot.
And the traditional system that we live in
doesn't necessarily capture those moments.
So we've got the ability to build new software
and new artifacts that will help us to actually capture
some of that.
All right.
Let's keep moving here.
This is a picture of a hackathon.
This is an interesting story because I didn't do particularly
well in molecular and cellular biology and chemistry or any
of the things that this hackathon in San Francisco
was about.
But the students used the Replit platform in order
to find biomarkers, in order to do things around drug discovery,
to do some life sciences innovation.
And my commentary to them as a judge, one of the many judges,
was about how deeply they thought about the solution,
how many people they surveyed.
Their process, a little bit more than my domain expertise.
And I think all of us, even if we don't go deep
into a particular area or domain,
can offer our lived experience and our perspective
to make the stuff that students are building a little bit
better.
All right.
This is the hand of a high school student in Chicago,
15 years old, named Jack.
He comes to school from 25, 30 miles outside
of where the school is actually at.
And the principal of Holy Trinity High School
gave students access to Replit this last spring.
And Jack decided to take the school's disciplines
and the things that they hold high in terms of the school
principles.
And he built out this system that he gave to teachers.
And teachers are able to identify
things that align with the school's values and principles.
And literally, the teachers can use their mobile phones
to basically reward and say, yes, that's exactly the exemplar
behavior or the care and the collaboration
that we want to encourage.
So literally changing the environment
and the culture of the school.
And they use the digital signage,
as students are walking in from the buses into the lobby
every morning, in order to show a leaderboard of sorts
of the students that are getting--
he put XPs.
So the students are getting XP in this application
on the digital signage, and they're
getting the positive reinforcement
that they all seek.
And you can use your XP that you accumulate in order
to do special things in this high school.
So this whole gamification and this idea
of the culture of the school being improved and enhanced
on the back of a vibe coding platform
was something that was a really cool thing
that I heard in our Chicago stop of the AI literacy tour.
All right.
And then when I asked Jack about how
he thought about learning AI, this
is how he broke it down for me.
He said learning with AI, so using it
as a tutor, collaborator, critic, translator.
He talked to me about learning about AI.
So they have one teacher in the entire school that
did a deep dive, a professional development, about a year ago,
and then brought what he learned to the sophomores, juniors,
